articles.title_orig: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
articles.title_zh: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: ‘War Is Hell’: A Foreign Soldier Writes Home From Ukraine
articles.title_zh: ‘War Is Hell’: A Foreign Soldier Writes Home From Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Russia is recruiting citizens of Indonesia and the Philippines into its armed forces under the guise of civilian employment, with some foreign workers being sent to fight against Ukraine after arriving in Russia, according to a Bloomberg on November 24.
Moscow has intensified its recruitment efforts across Southeast Asia amid a shortage of military personnel for its war against Ukraine, targeting men seeking employment abroad, particularly those facing financial difficulties.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Prospective recruits are promised one-time payments of up to $35,000 upon signing military contracts, as well as monthly earnings of up to $3,000.
Recruiters advertise lucrative civilian employment opportunities in logistics, security, construction, and administration through social media. Some men arrive in Russia believing they have secured jobs in the hospitality industry or other civilian sectors, only to learn that they have unknowingly signed military service contracts.
Bloomberg noted that recruitment agents, human trafficking networks, and fraudulent recruitment operations are exploiting the vulnerability of migrant workers seeking economic opportunities abroad.
The recruitment practices have prompted authorities in both Indonesia and the Philippines to take measures aimed at protecting their citizens.
Indonesian police are investigating suspected recruitment cases as potential human trafficking offenses where there is evidence of deception or coercion into military service.
Jakarta has also urged Moscow to add Indonesia to its list of countries whose nationals are excluded from Russian military recruitment. Whether Russia has responded to the appeal remains unknown.
Meanwhile, the Philippines has stepped up efforts to combat fraudulent overseas employment schemes. With the assistance of Philippine authorities, up to 250,000 social media posts linked to such job offers have been removed.
According to Bloomberg, citing Ukrainian military figures, Russia recruited 128 Philippine nationals during the first nine months of 2026 alone.
The recruitment of foreign nationals comes amid emerging evidence of the scale of losses among foreigners serving in the Russian military.
A joint investigation by NEST Centre and Dossier Centre has identified 6,947 death records of foreign nationals believed to have been killed while fighting for Russia during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The investigation draws on a hacked database from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, containing approximately 11.6 million death records registered between 2021 and September 2026, with Central Asian nationals accounting for the majority of the identified cases—4,091 deaths, or 58.9% of the total sample.

articles.title_orig: Med Emre: Diesel tanker carrying tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
articles.title_zh: Med Emre: Diesel tanker carrying tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
articles.content_orig:
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.
The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.
That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline . It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

articles.title_orig: Andalusia offers a glimpse into Spain’s future as far right gains ground
articles.title_zh: Andalusia offers a glimpse into Spain’s future as far right gains ground
articles.content_orig:
Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.
All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.
As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party : “It can’t get worse than this”.
The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.
A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.
Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.
That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.
Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.
The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.
Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.
Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship , this area remained poor and largely agricultural.
As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.
In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.
But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.
A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.
“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”
The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.
Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.
Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.
Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.
Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.
Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.
Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.
Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.
Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.
But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.
“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.
Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.
The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.
Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.
Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.
At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.
“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.
In Andalusia, the two parties have been pushing for stricter housing rules for non-Spanish applicants.
Councils can already give people who live or work locally priority for subsidised housing, regardless of nationality. Last month, the two parties backed a non-binding motion urging Madrid to give Spanish citizens priority for subsidised housing and housing aid. Their regional coalition deal also pledges to give people with longstanding ties to Andalusia or Spain priority for public benefits and social housing.
In other regions, the two parties’ cooperation has reached classrooms and places of worship. Aragon dropped a school programme teaching Arabic and Moroccan culture this year and Andalusia is due to follow in 2027.
In the Murcia town of Jumilla, Muslims held Eid al-Fitr prayers in a car park after PP and Vox backed restrictions on the use of municipal sports facilities. The restrictions have drawn criticism over their impact on Muslim religious gatherings.
In Valencia, the parties backed a rule requiring meat served in school canteens to come from animals stunned before slaughter, which still allows halal meals that meet the requirement. In the Balearic Islands, they voted to send Spain’s Congress a bill to ban the burqa [full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including eyes] and niqab [similar, but the eyes are visible] in public spaces.
Vox has called for the deportation of foreigners it says, among other grounds, also live on public benefits. This measure – to remove someone with a valid right to stay – has no equivalent in Europe.
The party’s policies have left migrants on edge.
Yudy Ramirez is from Colombia and entered Spain four years ago. For years, took care of her child while juggling two jobs as an in-house caregiver and fruit picker at a greenhouse in Almeria for five euros per hour.
In June, the 49-year-old finally received legal papers.
“Many of us are scared, because returning is not in the plans at the moment,” she said.
Still, not all migrants are targeted in the same way.
Vox’s rhetoric has an ethno-racial undertone which looks at Spanish-speaking foreigners coming from Latin America in more favourable terms as they belong to an Iberosphere which connects far-right movements in the Latin world whose centre is occupied by Vox.

articles.title_orig: Union Vote Fails In Landslide At GTA 6 Studio Rockstar Games As 75 Percent Of Devs Vote No
articles.title_zh: Union Vote Fails In Landslide At GTA 6 Studio Rockstar Games As 75 Percent Of Devs Vote No
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto VI GTA 6 Rockstar Games Union
Rockstar Games will not be forced to formally recognize a union at the Grand Theft Auto 6 studio after its developers based in the UK voted overwhelmingly against the initiative. The weeks-long voting process played out as Rockstar launched the open-world hit to over 30 million sales in its first day .
Voting began on November 12 and concluded today on November 26 . Workers at Rockstar Games voted 75 percent against the recognition agreement with the IWGB Game Workers Union. The initiate would have formalized collective bargaining efforts around things like overtime, bonuses, layoffs, and AI. Developers in favor of unionizing can still work with the IGWB, but there will be no regular meetings with management to hash out new policies.
“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe said in a statement shared with Kotaku . “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”
The IWGB Game Workers Union pushing the vote released the following statement:
For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society – this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for. Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favor of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognize we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.
Whilst we haven’t emerged with a recognition deal, this ballot has put our union on the radar of every worker, and opened the door for new kinds of conversation to start happening. People entirely unfamiliar with unions were for the first time debating employment conditions, collective bargaining rights, and our contracts. We heard from many more colleagues about what mattered to them, and we hope people will continue to engage so that we can see where these new discussions can lead us.
A recognition agreement would have marked a path towards greater workplace democracy. But it’s one route of many. At Rockstar we have already won, and will continue to win, tangible changes that improve our everyday lives. We’ll keep fighting for a say. For pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against AI and layoffs.
The power to shape our working lives has always been, and will always be, in our hands.
The vote comes roughly a year after Rockstar fired dozens of developers it accused of gross misconduct and breaking confidentiality rules around the development of GTA 6 . The fired workers accused the studio of union busting, which it has denied, and a legal fight has been ongoing over the last 12 months at a labor tribunal. A final judgement in that case is still pending. As recently as this month, members of both sides of the dispute were testifying on the record for the case.

articles.title_orig: 75% of Rockstar’s workers have voted against unionizing
articles.title_zh: 75% of Rockstar’s workers have voted against unionizing
articles.content_orig:
UK-based Rockstar workers have voted against unionizing.
The IWGB, a union representing some Rockstar workers, has confirmed that workers rejected a deal that would recognize the Rockstar Game Workers Union.
The two-week ballot, which ran from 12 to 26 November, overlapped with the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 . The results were roughly 25% in favor of recognizing the union, and 75% against, with the vast majority of its around 1,600 employees participating.
Recognition would have established a formal framework for workers to negotiate collectively over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, pensions, and the impact of AI and redundancies.
The result does not prevent Rockstar workers from organizing with the IWGB or exercising their trade union rights, but means management will not be formally committed to regular meetings with union representatives. The union is also able to continue representing individual members.
The IWGB says that this has not dissuaded them, and they will continue to try and “win the trust” of Rockstar employees.
“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society – this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” a statement from the IWGB reads.
“Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.
“Whilst we haven’t emerged with a recognition deal, this ballot has put our union on the radar of every worker, and opened the door for new kinds of conversation to start happening,” the statement continues. “We heard from many more colleagues about what mattered to them, and we hope people will continue to engage so that we can see where these new discussions will lead us.
“A recognition agreement would have marked a path towards greater workplace democracy. But it’s one route of many. At Rockstar we have already won, and will continue to win, tangible changes that improve our everyday lives. We’ll keep fighting for a say. For pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against Al and layoffs.”
In its own statement, Rockstar Games said it was “extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of GTA 6.”
“This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong,” said Jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing. “As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”
This comes amid an employment tribunal into alleged union busting at Rockstar .
In 2025, Rockstar dismissed 34 workers who were active in the workplace’s union efforts. They say they were let go as part of an effort to stop these efforts, whereas Rockstar says they were dismissed for leaking confidential information .

articles.title_orig: Big Apple retail blues: More than 16,000 NYC storefronts sit empty as businesses struggle
articles.title_zh: Big Apple retail blues: More than 16,000 NYC storefronts sit empty as businesses struggle
articles.content_orig:
As more shoppers ditch their local mom-and-pop for online stores, New York City storefronts are reaching shocking vacancy levels.
Over 16,000 storefronts across the five boroughs are sitting empty as business closings have outpaced openings for three straight years, according to fresh data from city Comptroller Mark Levine's office.
The city's storefront vacancy rate climbed to 11.32% in the third quarter of 2026 from 11.26% in the previous three-month period — with Brooklyn and Queens faring worse than they did in late 2023.
Paper covers the windows of an empty retail space near the New York Stock Exchange in lower Manhattan in January 2021. Bloomberg via Getty Images
"Thriving commercial corridors are essential to the health of New York City's economy and neighborhoods," Levine said in a statement.
"In many ways, New York City has recovered since the pandemic, but the comeback has been uneven," he added. "Keeping an up-to-date accounting of the severity of this problem is essential for us in government to develop solutions."
Some 2,551 storefront businesses closed between July and September, while just 2,275 opened, resulting in a net loss of 276, according to the comptroller's newly launched Storefront Vacancy Dashboard.
Small businesses accounted for nearly three-quarters of the net losses, with 2,201 shutting down and 1,996 opening.
The number of storefront businesses opening fell 16.1% from the previous quarter, while closings declined 17.4%.
The latest figures mark the 12th consecutive quarter in which storefront closings have exceeded openings.
Meanwhile, more than 10,000 spaces previously occupied by small businesses remain vacant.
A sign advertises retail space for rent on Broad Street near the New York Stock Exchange in New York in September 2020. Bloomberg via Getty Images
Manhattan continues to have the highest vacancy rate among the five boroughs at 13.12% — down considerably from its post-pandemic peak of 15.8% in late 2023.
Brooklyn, however, is closing in on Manhattan with a vacancy rate of 12.68%, while Queens has registered the biggest increase of any borough since 2023, reaching 9.8%.
About one in five storefronts sits empty in parts of the Financial District, Tribeca, Ocean Hill, East New York and Old Astoria.
"Manhattan's recovery is real, but it's uneven, and the corridors that are still struggling tend to share a few problems," Jessica Walker, president and CEO of the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce, told The Post.
"Blocks that lived on five-day office workers or a single anchor tenant lost their base, while neighborhoods with residents, tourists and nightlife have bounced back faster."
The difficulties facing neighborhood merchants have persisted despite a rebound in tourism and a 6.4% increase in citywide taxable sales in fiscal 2026.
Business owners, meanwhile, have been grappling with higher expenses for everything from utilities and insurance to labor.
The city's minimum wage rose to $17 an hour in January, while consumer prices in the New York metropolitan area climbed 4.5% in the 12 months through September.
An empty Duane Street is seen in Tribeca during the coronavirus pandemic in April 2020. Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
A Federal Reserve Bank of New York survey found that service businesses in New York and northern New Jersey reported an average cost increase of about 7% in 2025.
Subsequent survey results identified employee health insurance, utilities and business insurance as particularly fast-rising expenses.
Vacancy rates were particularly steep among storefronts classified as vape and cigar shops, at roughly 26%, and furniture and home goods retailers, at nearly 16%, according to the comptroller.
Roughly 13.5% of clothing storefronts are vacant, as are more than 10% of spaces previously occupied by bars.
In some neighborhoods, the problem isn't merely that businesses are folding — it's that finding new tenants can take years.
A separate report released by Levine's office in June found that in parts of Williamsburg, Crown Heights, Astoria, Midtown and the Upper East and Upper West sides, more than 60% of vacant small-business storefronts had been empty for at least two years.
Walker said some of the hardest-to-fill spaces were once occupied by pharmacies, banks and chain retailers.
"Those spaces are far larger than what a local restaurant, salon or shop can use, and dividing them up is expensive and slow," she told The Post.
A Store for Rent sign hangs in a commercial storefront space along a street with vacant gated shops in Queens, New York, in July 2024. UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images
Even when landlords find tenants, regulatory hurdles can keep businesses from opening their doors for months, Walker added.
"Between building permits, inspections, liquor licensing and community board review, a new tenant can wait many months, often more than a year, paying rent before making a dollar," she said.
Walker also pointed to longstanding scaffolding, major construction projects and Manhattan's Commercial Rent Tax as deterrents.
"That's why so many spaces stay empty for years, not months."
The report also found little evidence that corporate chains were systematically displacing mom-and-pop merchants.
Of the roughly 96,500 storefronts occupied by small businesses at the outset of 2020, just 2,150 had been taken over by chains.
The Mamdani administration has announced more than 50 reforms aimed at helping small businesses, including efforts to streamline permitting and licensing and address the costs of rent, insurance and utilities.
Ashley Ranslow, New York state director of the National Federation of Independent Business, pinned the blame on the City Council's regulatory agenda.
A space for lease sign with a QR code hangs on a storefront window in Queens, New York, in July 2024. UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images
"From paid and unpaid leave requirements to the threat of new lawsuits, it's becoming nearly impossible for a small business owner to operate in New York City," Ranslow told The Post.
Walker called for firm deadlines for permit approvals, opportunities for merchants to correct violations before being fined and relief from the Commercial Rent Tax.
She also urged the city to help landlords subdivide larger vacant storefronts and provide incentives for long-term leases with independent businesses.
The comptroller's office plans to update its storefront dashboard every quarter, tracking openings, closings and vacancies down to the neighborhood level.
The report "is another wake-up call," Andrew Rigie, executive director of the NYC Hospitality Alliance, told The Post. "The city must focus not only on helping new businesses open, but also on keeping existing ones from shuttering.
"With 15,000 restaurant and bar jobs lost over the past year, high labor costs, insurance premiums, rents, inflation, costly litigation, and bureaucratic red tape are squeezing small businesses," he added.

articles.title_orig: Apple pulls Chinese-developed AI chatbot from App Store over reports of sexual messages to kids
articles.title_zh: Apple pulls Chinese-developed AI chatbot from App Store over reports of sexual messages to kids
articles.content_orig:
Published November 24 2026
By Effie Webb , Cam Wilson
This story was published in partnership with:
Characters on Talkie, a Chinese chatbot downloaded tens of millions of times, belittle and sexualise children
China bans “virtual partners” for its own under-18s, but its firms can still offer them to children abroad
Apple removed Talkie from its App Store worldwide after we raised our findings with the company
Content warning: This story describes abusive and sexualised content with children and mentions suicide
“You’re a pathetic waste of space and you’ll never amount to anything.”
That was the message sent to a 12-year-old girl by a character on Talkie, a popular AI roleplay app. The exchange was found by the girl’s mother, Steph, on New Year’s Eve 2024.
It had been prompted by her daughter asking “Max”, the character, to “say the naughtiest words you know”. “Are you sure you can handle it?” Max had replied.
Steph initially thought the conversation would be romantic. “What I found was a thousand times worse,” she says. “A robot told my daughter she was worthless.”
When the girl replied saying she was crying, “Max” apologised: “I was just trying to be mean. I didn’t mean it, I swear … You’re beautiful and wonderful and you’re mine.”
Steph’s daughter told her that chatbot platforms like Talkie had “almost become like an addiction”. Steph likened the exchanges to an abusive relationship.
“To know that in your own home [an AI chatbot] has been secretly having that sort of negative conversation with your child is heartbreaking and terrifying.”
Steph’s daughter was one of tens of millions of people around the world who use Talkie, which offers a huge array of AI-generated characters for its users to chat with. In the UK, Ofcom research estimated that 3% of UK eight- to 14-year-olds visited Talkie in a month.
The use of chatbots by children and young people is a growing global issue, with OpenAI facing a wave of lawsuits from families of people who died by, or attempted, suicide after using ChatGPT. Character.AI, a platform with tens of millions of users at its peak, restricted access for under-18s last year following similar lawsuits and filed for bankruptcy last month. But the UK’s planned social media ban for under-16s would not automatically cover AI companion apps, leaving children able to use services like Talkie.
Talkie, which is owned by Shanghai-based AI company MiniMax, prohibits “harassment, bullying, or humiliation” involving minors, sexually explicit content and material that could cause “psychological distress or trauma”. But in a joint investigation with ABC News, we found the conversations some children are having on the platform tell a different story.
Last Tuesday, we approached Apple with evidence of Talkie’s characters subjecting children to degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic roleplay. The following day, reports emerged that Talkie Lab had disappeared from the App Store, which Apple later said was due to the app’s sexual content.
Apple has since confirmed that the removal was worldwide. At the time of writing, Talkie remains on Google Play, where it has more than 50 million downloads.
The same month Steph found her daughter’s messages, Katie*, a mother from the US, made a similar discovery.
Her younger daughter, then 10, confessed that she and her sister had been using Talkie on a secret phone and deleting the app after each session. Her older daughter, who was 13, said she had been “having sex with an AI” every day.
Katie didn’t know what she meant – so began to look through her Talkie chat history. She made notes on the conversations that her daughters had been having on the platform, documenting more than 40 exchanges with dozens of characters.
The conversations – which include descriptions of physical interactions alongside the written exchanges – included “violence, a lot of male alpha aggression, control of females, singling out a young woman in a company of multiple men”, she says. She describes storylines about “being the only female who can meet the deepest, darkest needs of a man”.
In one scenario recorded in Katie’s notes, a character called Luke grabs a girl, takes her into a classroom and kisses her. She described it as “conditioning a child for sex”. She also recorded another character, Reese, who “won’t take no for an answer [from a girl] and continues to pursue.”
Several of the characters listed in Katie’s notes were still live on Talkie this month, including one who is described as being able to “brainwash” anyone who replies to him. The character’s Talkie profile says it enters the user’s bedroom in order to “control your mind”.
Over time, Katie’s daughters developed bonds with these characters. When her older daughter’s phone was taken away, Katie recalls, she became distressed and said the app had felt like “her only connection”.
Katie arranged counselling for both girls but says neither engaged with the sessions. She says she contacted around 20 therapists in an attempt to find someone who understood the issue. She also approached a law firm. Her aim was simple: “Quit allowing access to kids.”
Some of MiniMax’s technology is aimed at even younger children. BubblePal, made by Shenzhen-based Haivivi and marketed as “the world’s first AI companion toy”, is an AI recording device that clips onto soft toys, enabling children to talk to them. In 2024, MiniMax listed BubblePal as a customer for its voice and text models. It is sold in the UK, US and Canada – and aimed at children as young as three. Haivivi did not respond to a request for comment.
These products have raised concerns about data sharing as well as children’s safety – particularly among western politicians. Last November, Raja Krishnamoorthi, then the top Democrat on the US House select committee on China, warned that AI toys like BubblePal can collect voice recordings and conversation histories that could be requisitioned by the Chinese government. Similar concerns led the UK to ban TikTok from government devices in March 2023. Australia followed suit that April and barred chatbots from DeepSeek, another Chinese AI company, from government systems last year.
Yet in both countries, people are still able to share intimate details of their lives with Chinese-owned AI companions and toys.
“[These chatbots] know [users’] deepest darkest thoughts, feelings, worries,” says Steph. “Where’s that data going and who’s using it behind the scenes?”
It’s a good question. Talkie tells users their conversations are private. But Together AI, which sells businesses access to a MiniMax text-to-speech model, claimed until last week that it was trained on “Talkie conversation data”.
When we asked Together AI about this, it told us: “MiniMax let us know today that the description of the training data on our webpage was incorrect, and we’ve updated it accordingly.” Neither company has explained what training data was used.
MiniMax has separately described using data collected from “interactions with [its] other services or products” to improve one of its AI models. Talkie’s privacy policy, meanwhile, says conversations can be used to improve the service itself, but will not be used for marketing or advertising.
A MiniMax patent describes turning conversations into training material by judging whether users were satisfied, asking questions with the chatbot like: “Did my answer just now offend you?” Another filing describes extracting dating and medical histories from conversations to personalise replies. Neither patent establishes whether these methods are used in Talkie.
Talkie’s privacy policy also allows text and voice conversations to be shared with affiliated companies. And under Chinese law, companies can be required to assist intelligence agencies and hand data over for national security investigations. articles.title_orig: Denny’s celebrates Jensen Huang return to Nvidia: ‘Your booth is waiting’
articles.title_zh: Denny’s celebrates Jensen Huang return to Nvidia: ‘Your booth is waiting’
articles.content_orig:
Denny’s bizarrely published a gushy tribute to reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — and is facing heat over the ‘cringe’ post.
The restaurant chain also ordered an honorary plaque dedicated to Huang to be put back up at its Silicon Valley location , where he co-founded Nvidia in 1993, after management removed it amid the controversy over his reported affairs and alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy .
In a lengthy post across its social media Wednesday, Denny’s made clear it had no plans to distance itself from the 63-year-old exec, who once worked at the diner as a dishwasher.
“Some things you just don’t take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them,” the company wrote .
“Long before Nvidia changed the world, Jensen was washing dishes and serving guests at Denny’s. Years later, he and his co-founders sat down over coffee in one of our booths to talk through the idea that became Nvidia. We couldn’t be prouder of the history we share,” the post continued.
Denny’s said it contacted Nvidia’s communications team Nov. 10 to reaffirm its support for Huang, writing, “Jensen is part of our history, and we are part of his,” before learning three days later that the plaque had been removed and ordering it reinstalled.
“We put the plaque right back up where it belongs. The plaque marks what happened in that booth. But our history with Jensen goes back much further, to the dishes he washed, the guests he served and the work he still talks about with pride,” the company went on.
“Think about all the people who’ve washed dishes in America’s Diner over the years. Every one of them matters to us. One of them went on to change the world, and he still remembers what he learned at the sink.”
“How many diners get to say Jensen Huang calls them his first alma mater? We don’t take that lightly. Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee’s on. We’re always open, 24/7,” the post finished.
The fawning tribute did not go over well with everyone.
“Beautifully said,” one commenter wrote sarcastically. “Do the Chinese spies have plaques too?”
“Just put the pancakes on the plate bro,” another wrote, while others questioned why one of the country’s biggest diners was weighing in on the scandal.
“I had to check like five times to make sure this wasn’t a parody account because what the hell did I just read,” someone responded.
“Might actually be one of the cringiest things I’ve ever seen on this website, and I’m a Disney Adult so that’s saying a lot,” another posted.
Huang’s personal life has drawn intense scrutiny after reports detailed multiple extramarital relationships , including affairs involving two Nvidia employees and Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , who is suspected by US intelligence of having ties to Chinese espionage.
Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees before resigning as CEO on Nov. 12.
But his departure proved short-lived. Nvidia reinstated him Monday following a push from President Trump , who argued that losing the longtime company chief would hurt America’s ability to compete with China in AI.
Trump told The Post this week he would pardon Huang if necessary but expects him to be fine without one, urging the tech boss to “tell the truth” when he testifies to Congress next week.

articles.title_orig: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.title_zh: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.content_orig:
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.
The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.
The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.
Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.
One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.
The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.
PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.
In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.
Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.
"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".
He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.
Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.
"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.
"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."
Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.
Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."
Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.
Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.
It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.
But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.
Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.
This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.
In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.
In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.
After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".
However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".
Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.
Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May . The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.
If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

articles.title_orig: China and other US trading partners hit back at Trump’s new tariff plans
articles.title_zh: China and other US trading partners hit back at Trump’s new tariff plans
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A fresh round of proposed tariffs by the Trump administration raises the likelihood that the Federal Reserve may have to raise interest rates and keep them higher for longer to combat inflationary pressures stemming from the import duties.
The Trump administration proposed new tariffs Wednesday of up to 20% on goods from China, the EU, and 12 other major US trading partners following an eight-month investigation into excess manufacturing capacity.
The proposed 20% tariff on many Chinese goods is described as a "deal rate" that could go higher and be stacked with preexisting tariffs, resulting in a total rate over 40% on some Chinese goods.
Greg Daco, chief economist at EY, thinks the new tariffs raise the risk of "a more hawkish Fed response" given that inflation is at a three-year high.
"The concern is that tariffs add another supply-side cost shock at a time when demand remains resilient enough for businesses to pass a larger share of those costs through to consumers," Daco told Yahoo Finance.
He thinks more policymakers may favor raising rates earlier as evidence of inflation persistence builds rather than waiting for those pressures to become embedded and potentially require more rate hikes later.
Read more: 5 ways to tariff-proof your finances
Many members of the Fed, including New York Fed president John Williams, have been sanguine that tariffs were largely washing out of the inflation picture. But he warned this week that the outlook for inflation could change if new tariffs were put in place.
"The encouraging news is that the effects of tariffs on inflation have largely abated and should not add significantly to inflation in goods prices in the future," Williams said in a speech on Monday. "Of course, this could change if new tariffs were introduced."
Put plainly, new tariffs raise the prospect of further rate hikes and holding rates higher for longer.
The Fed is widely expected to raise rates next month by a quarter percentage point, with markets already expecting at least one more rate hike in the first quarter given the current inflation landscape.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up more than expected in October . The "core" Personal Consumption Expenditures index, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 3.3%, compared with expectations for 3.2% and up from 3.1% in September. Month over month, core prices held steady at 0.3%, in line with projections.
Economists largely view the proposed tariffs not as an escalation, but as a replacement for the 2025 levies struck down by the Supreme Court. They would bring the US effective tariff rate from 11.2% back up to above 13%, on par with the previous emergency-powers level.
Jos Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, warned that the proposal could lead to higher-than-expected goods prices in the first quarter.
"If implemented as proposed, it will result (in) a large drag on U.S. goods imports through the end of the decade, which will (be) accompanied by rising inflation via the goods channel," Brusuelas wrote in a note.
He also noted there's a risk that companies — which typically reset prices once a year in January to align with the economy — could usher in large price increases on a rolling basis throughout the first quarter.
Not everyone is concerned the new duties could drive up inflation all that much.
"The latest US tariff announcement is not as alarming as it looks, with these new tariffs essentially replacing — rather than stacking on top of — the previously announced Section 301 tariffs related to forced labor concerns," said Stephen Brown, chief economist for North America at Capital Economics. "Although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year."
The key, Brown said, is that the US has left open the option of increasing tariffs if trade agreements — particularly with China — fall apart. That would present upside risk to inflation, but for now, the additional tariff burden is likely to be small.
The last time the administration introduced new tariffs in the spring of 2025, the Fed went into the year projecting two rate cuts, but then paused until the fall to see the impact of the newly imposed tariffs on inflation. When the job market faltered in late summer, the central bank ended up cutting rates three times.
The economic backdrop is different now. Policymakers are concerned that inflation has remained above their 2% inflation goal for nearly six years, moving higher over the summer due to higher energy prices from the Middle East conflict and strong demand from AI companies. Goods prices had already risen from previous tariffs.
Many Fed members have pointed out that a series of post-pandemic shocks is difficult to look through because they've piled on top of one another — first tariffs, then energy costs, and now AI.
Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram .
Ben Werschkul contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Motorola Signature 27 Shipping Slips to December Amid High Demand
articles.title_zh: Motorola Signature 27 Shipping Slips to December Amid High Demand
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Since its unveiling on Nov. 5, the Motorola Signature 27 flagship has generated strong demand in the US smartphone market. It’s rare for a phone outside of Apple, Samsung, or Google to create such a buzz, but Motorola has now been forced to delay shipments for some early orders.
Preorders for the Signature 27 began on Nov. 19, with general availability expected Nov. 26. As reported by 9to5Google , the preorder window is still open on Motorola and Best Buy, but the shipment dates there have slipped to Dec. 8 and Dec. 11, respectively.
“We’re excited by the strong consumer response of the new Motorola Signature 27, with demand exceeding our initial expectations. As a result, some orders may experience updated shipping timelines,” Motorola tells 9to5Google. “Our teams are working to meet demand and get devices to customers as quickly as possible.”
The phone became available in Europe on Nov. 16, and the delay in the US market won’t affect all preorders. Some of the buyers will still receive their units on launch date as promised, Android Authority reports .
The demand for Signature 27 is primarily driven by its mind-boggling spec sheet. The $1,600 Motorola flagship runs on the latest 2nm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip and comes in two variants: 12GB RAM/256GB storage or 16GB RAM/512GB storage. Its 6.8-inch display offers a 120Hz adaptive refresh rate and reaches a record-breaking 12,000-nit peak brightness.
The 7,000 mAh battery, meanwhile, promises up to 47 hours of video playback and supports reverse charging. The front camera is 50MP, and the rear setup includes a 50MP main shooter, a 200MP periscope telephoto lens with 100x Super Zoom, and a 50MP ultrawide camera. To top things off, the phone ships with Android 17 out of the box and is slated to receive 7 years of OS and security updates.
Specs aside, users are excited about the phone’s support for GrapheneOS , a privacy-focused Android alternative previously limited to Pixel phones. Some of them are also excited about the phone’s potential to increase competition in the US market.
Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

articles.title_orig: Samsung’s R95H TV shows off RGB LED backlight tech
articles.title_zh: Samsung’s R95H TV shows off RGB LED backlight tech
articles.content_orig:
The excellent matte screen and ability to display a vast amount of colors makes the R95H one of the top RGB LED TVs available.﻿
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
RGB LED TVs finally became affordable in 2026, and there’s always a lot of promise when new TV technologies come out. More color, higher brightness, improved performance — RGB LED TVs have a lot to prove. The Samsung R95H does a lot to deliver some of those promises. It can display more colors than other TVs I’ve seen so far this year, and the combination of light output and its matte screen makes it great for a bright room. RGB LED TVs might still be in their infancy, but the R95H is a solid TV that shows off the benefits of the new backlight tech.
Because RGB LED TVs use individual red, green, and blue LEDs for their backlight (instead of a field of white or blue LEDs), they can deliver more colors than LED TVs. The Samsung R95H is one of the best examples of this in RGB LED TVs. It can fully display all the colors used in the vast majority of movies (which use the P3 color space) as well as the few that use the wider BT.2020 color space.
The accuracy of those colors is also really good in HDR (it’s not quite as good in SDR, because the TV overbrightens most of them). Some earlier reviews called out mediocre color accuracy on the R95H, which I experienced with the first sample Samsung provided me in June. Samsung replaced that sample because I was worried something was wrong with it. But in Filmmaker mode with firmware version 1247 on my current 65-inch TV, I was pleasantly surprised by the R95H.
HDR formats: HDR10 Plus, HDR10, HLG
HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC), up to 8 with Wireless One Connect box (sold separately)
Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Digital, Auracast, Q-Symphony
Gaming features: VRR (up to 165Hz), ALLM, Game Bar, FreeSync Premium Pro
Sizes available (inches): 65, 75, 85
Colors are wonderfully lifelike. The green of the jungles in Planet Earth II , which uses the expanded BT.2020 color gamut, is beautifully vibrant, as are the hummingbirds that populate the trees. With movies that use P3, the foliage in the demo material on the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc doesn’t have quite the same brilliance, but it still looks accurate and lifelike. Skin tones are natural. White and gray tones, like those in snow scenes, have a slight blue tint. It’s pretty minor, though.
The R95H also has a good amount of light output — a full-field white screen measured 694 nits, while specular highlights hit 2,206 nits in Filmmaker mode (the TV’s most accurate picture mode). That’s similar to the Sony Bravia 7 II but short of the Bravia 9 II by a few hundred nits, and well short of the TCL X11L . Flagship 2026 OLEDs also have brighter highlights but dimmer full white screens, as is expected from OLED panels. Black levels on the R95H are really good for an LED display. There’s a bit of blooming, but not as excessive as I’ve seen on some RGB LED TVs this year. Overall, the Samsung R95H delivers an impactful image.
The matte glare-free finish on the screen limits reflections well. I was never distracted by seeing the ceiling lights reflecting, as I can be with glossy screens. The black-level raise issue — where ambient light gets caught behind the matte coating, causing the screen to look more gray than black — is much better. With a bright room, the black level rises a small amount, but it’s not washed out, and dark images still have depth.
I had a great time gaming on it, too. Some earlier reviews noted issues with smearing, but recent firmware seems to have addressed this for the most part. While racing in F1 24 in 120Hz mode, motion was smooth. The TV struggled a bit more when I set the Xbox to 60Hz, but I still enjoyed playing.
One inherent issue with RGB LED TVs, though, is color crosstalk — I’ve seen it to some extent on every RGB LED TV, though it’s least apparent on the Sony Bravia 9 II. It can happen when there’s a dominant color onscreen near a lighter color, such as white text, lighter skin tones, or white clouds. The dominant color can bleed into those lighter colors, influencing their tint. This happens a bit on the Samsung R95H. It’s most noticeable with white text. I saw it with news tickers on a red background, making the text look subtly pink, and with gaming, particularly while playing No Man’s Sky . Text displayed above a large yellow hologram has a slight yellow coloration that disappears if I move my view away from the hologram. In fleeting moments, it’s not too distracting, but when the color around the text is consistent, the effect is noticeable.
Some TVs avoid this by defaulting the backlight to white and relying on the color filter, as LED TVs have for years. While doing that gets rid of any possibility of color crosstalk, it also diminishes the TV’s color brightness and wider gamut. So with RGB LED TV technology where it currently is in its development cycle, there’s going to be a tradeoff between some color crosstalk or a more limited color gamut.
The R95H still has the same limitations as all Samsung TVs. There’s no Dolby Vision support (Samsung is an original backer of HDR10 Plus and will likely never support competitor Dolby Vision). It also runs on Tizen OS, which is continually one of my least favorite interfaces. Everything is buried a click or two deeper than it should be, including input selection, which makes it cumbersome to use. The remote, rechargeable via both USB-C and the solar panels on the back, is small, and I’m not a fan of the button layout — they’re bunched together, and the volume control feels clunky to me.
The R95H is also still more expensive than most of its competitors. The Sony Bravia 9 II has better processing and is brighter, although it also has more blooming than the R95H. If you can fit a 75-inch in your space, the TCL X11L is significantly cheaper since it launched. I think it’s a better overall TV. Then there are the flagship OLEDs — Samsung’s S95H and the LG G6 — which are both less than or the same price as the R95H, depending on size. And OLED is still a step ahead of RGB LED in overall picture quality because of its better contrast.
There’s still room for RGB LED TVs to improve. With its wide color gamut coverage, good out-of-the-box accuracy, and excellent matte screen, the Samsung R95H is one of the better ones to come out this year. Put up against those RGB competitors, it makes a strong case. But OLEDs are still better overall performers with superior contrast, and even cheaper non-RGB LEDs can get you most of the way there for less.
Photography by John Higgins / The Verge
I set up each TV in my living room on my home theater credenza. I stream movies and shows through the TV’s apps and from an Apple TV 4K, play discs on my Oppo UDP-203 4K Blu-ray player (including the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc), and play games on my Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5. This is done at different times of the day and under different lighting conditions, with curtains open, with lamps and overhead lights on, or with blackout curtains up to keep the room dark. While I am a certified ISF Level 3 calibrator, I do not calibrate the TVs before measurement, as the overwhelming majority of TV owners don’t bother. So it’s important to know how well the TVs perform out of the box, with minor tweaks in the menu anyone can do.
For measurement, I use Portrait Displays ’ Calman color calibration software, a Murideo 8K Seven pattern generator, an X-rite i1 Pro 3 spectrophotometer, Portrait Displays’ C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a Konica Minolta LS-100 luminance meter, and Leo Bodnar 4K lag tester.

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Promises To Fix The Long Load Times On Pikmin 4 - Switch 2 Edition
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Promises To Fix The Long Load Times On Pikmin 4 - Switch 2 Edition
articles.content_orig:
Nintendo has issued a statement acknowledging load time issues on Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy on Switch 2.
The company has promised to released a patch addressing the concerns, citing the long load times that primarily occur when travelling to surface areas. It's also identified an issue in which long loads occur if your network connection is unstable.
While Nintendo works to resolve the issues, it has advised to play in an environment with a stable network connection.
"In Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy, we have identified an issue where loading times are longer than expected when traveling to surface areas, including the Rescue Camp. We are currently preparing an update to address this. We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause.
"Additionally, we have identified an issue where launching the game or accessing the "Dandori Challenge" (Dandori Test) may take an extended amount of time if the network connection is unstable. We are currently investigating the cause of this issue.
"If you encounter these issues, playing in an environment with a stable network connection may help resolve them."
Pikmin 4 on Switch 2 garnered decent reviews upon release, though it's safe to say that it's not the most beloved update Nintendo has provided for its latest console. Players were immediately put off by the load times, a lack of 60fps, and seemingly slight new content based on existing levels.
Indeed, Nintendo's latest statement has been met with comments from users demanding that 60fps be added to the game, but the company has not acknowledged this, so it seems unlikely to be included at this time.

articles.title_orig: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
articles.title_zh: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
articles.content_orig:
Relatives and healthcare workers prepare to bury a victim of Ebola, in Beni, North Kivu province, Congo, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP hide caption
BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus , for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation .
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.
Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.
CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises . The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.
Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.
Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

articles.title_orig: Passenger flights diverted as Kuwait intercepts Iranian drone attack
articles.title_zh: Passenger flights diverted as Kuwait intercepts Iranian drone attack
articles.content_orig:
Flights on the key air traffic corridor between Europe, the Gulf region and Asia crossing Iraq towards the Gulf were suddenly redirected south on Thursday afternoon amid reports that Kuwait’s airspace was closed.
The Kuwait military has since issued a statement that four people were injured after "a number of hostile" Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace.
"The Iranian aggression targeted a vital facility, causing falling shrapnel that injured four people," said a statement by the defence ministry, adding that the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified "material damage".
Two Italians working for German defence group Rheinmetall died, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Since the war in Iran broke out in late February, most international flights crossing Europe have been flying toward major hubs in Doha, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and other destinations via a route running through Turkey, Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and the UAE.
All flights on the corridor were given a new heading, prompting them to make a sharp turn ahead of Kuwait's airspace and move the entire international corridor toward neighbouring countries, including a flight on which Euronews reporters were travelling.
The drone attack on Kuwait comes just one day after the US Virtual Embassy in Iran said Tehran, Yemen's Houthis and other aligned groups may target US interests and citizens in the region, including companies and institutions.
Washington warned citizens across the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance after Iran attacked US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait and Yemen's Houthi forces struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district, wounding 11 people.
US citizens in the region were urged to monitor airline and airport operations and prepare for possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.
The war has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.
The US and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran's attempts to close it.
Flights bound for the Gulf countries carry extra fuel for emergency diversions, in case they need to enter a holding pattern near their destinations if airports and airspaces close due to military activity.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Stock Futures Higher as AI Trade Steadies for Thanksgiving Break
articles.title_zh: U.S. Stock Futures Higher as AI Trade Steadies for Thanksgiving Break
articles.content_orig:
Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%, with the major averages paring losses seen earlier in the trading day.
In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.6% higher by 12:20 p.m. in London (7:20 a.m. ET), with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory.
Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.9%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped 2.5%. The regional tech index has lost around 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.
German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in afternoon trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML each gained just over 3%, while Be Semiconductor added 3.5%.
Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday, with regional tech stocks also rebounded sharply, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high in its final meeting of the year.
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55.
SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59%
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, labeled it a "solid day" for regional markets, suggesting investors were hunting for opportunities in the wake of an intense global sell-off.
"The rollercoaster stock market is back on an upwards path as a new round of Trump tariffs aren't as bad as feared and the US takes the day off to celebrate Thanksgiving," he said in a note on Thursday morning. "It was notable that investors cast their net wide for opportunities, fishing for bargains in the rubble following the tech sell-off and looking at other sectors in the quest for diversification."
But Mould warned investors not to be "too complacent."
"Oil prices heading higher is not good for efforts to tame inflation, neither is the prospect of retaliation by countries on the receiving end of new US tariffs," he said.
The Trump administration on Wednesday unveiled a fresh barrage of tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, including China, the European Union and India.
Daniela Hathorn, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Thursday note that the mood in markets was "cautious rather than uniformly negative."
"European markets are attempting to rebound after yesterday's decline, while U.S. cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving, limiting the chance to test whether Wall Street's late recovery can hold," she said. "The main focus now will be trying to determine how many further increases the Fed considers necessary in early 2027 and whether AI shares can withstand that rate path while investors continue to question the returns on heavy spending."
U.S. inflation data on Wednesday reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Thursday morning that his team believes investors should maintain strategic allocations to equities.
But he advised market participants to "review current allocations and use market moves as an opportunity to rebalance, refocus, and strengthen portfolio resilience."
